articles.title: Aura Test: Find Out What Your Aura Color Says About You | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: Not sure what an aura test actually measures? Here's how aura color tests work, what each color means, and how to figure out yours without a special device.
articles.answer: An aura test is a way of identifying which color best represents your energy and personality, according to the New Age tradition of aura reading. There's no scientific instrument involved — the “test” is really a self-assessment: you compare your traits and current mood against the traditional meaning of each aura color.
sections: How aura tests actually work

Most online "aura tests" are one of two things: a short quiz that asks about your habits and preferences and maps your answers to a color, or a plain description of each color that you compare yourself against. Neither involves any equipment — despite some claims online, there's no camera or app that photographs an actual aura.
The value isn't in precision, it's in reflection: reading through the traits tied to each color is a quick way to think about your own personality and current state of mind.
The main aura colors and what they mean

ul: Blue — calm, communicative, a natural listener.
Yellow — optimistic, creative, mentally energetic.
Green — balanced, grounded, drawn to harmony.
White — going through (or seeking) a major transition.
Red — passionate, decisive, high physical energy.
Purple — intuitive, spiritual, a rare aura color.
Pink — affectionate, empathetic, relationship-focused.
Black — introspective, protective, often tied to a period of rest.

sections: Want the full breakdown for each one? The aura color test walks through the traits behind every color in more detail.
Can your aura color change?

According to the tradition, yes. Your aura color reflects your current state as much as your baseline personality, so it's normal to feel like you identify with a different color depending on what you're going through — or with two colors at once.
faq: Is there a real device that reads auras?

No verified scientific instrument measures an aura. Some “aura photography” booths use biofeedback sensors (like skin temperature) mapped to colors for entertainment, but this isn't a validated measurement of anything paranormal.
What's the difference between an aura test and an aura color test?
They're the same idea. This page is a general overview of how aura reading works; the aura color test goes deeper into the specific traits tied to each color.

articles.title: Piccolo Aura Farming: The Anime Edit Trend Explained | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: Why Piccolo became the face of aura farming edits, plus the other anime and game characters that get the same treatment: Gojo, Sung Jin Woo, Agamemnon.
articles.answer: Piccolo aura farming refers to a wave of edits that pair calm, understated moments of the Dragon Ball character Piccolo with epic music, framing his composure as maximum “aura” — the same social-media shorthand for effortless carisma that spawned the aura farming meme in the first place.
sections: Why Piccolo specifically

Aura farming edits are built on contrast: someone doing something impressive while looking completely unbothered. Piccolo fits that template almost perfectly — he's known for standing still, saying little, and rarely raising his voice even in high-stakes moments. Editors slow down or freeze-frame his stillest scenes, add a dramatic soundtrack, and the result reads as pure "aura" by the meme's own logic: no visible effort, no reaction, no explanation.
It also helps that Piccolo has decades of source material to pull from, so there's no shortage of clips that fit the format.
Gojo, Sung Jin Woo, and Agamemnon

Piccolo isn't alone. A handful of other characters get the same edit treatment for the same reason — each one has a signature "calm despite overwhelming power" moment that fits the aura farming template:

ul: Gojo Satoru (Jujutsu Kaisen) — his casual confidence and one-liners in the middle of fights make him a favorite for this style of edit.
Sung Jin Woo (Solo Leveling) — his quiet, understated reactions to increasingly absurd power scaling are a near-perfect match for the format.
Agamemnon — another recurring pick in the same wave of "overpowered and unbothered" character edits.

sections: The common thread across all four: the character does something remarkable and the edit deliberately underplays it, which is exactly what "farming aura" means outside of anime too.
How this connects to the original meme

The anime edits and the original aura farming meme (which started with a real video of a kid dancing on a canoe in Indonesia) share the same rulebook: reacting with zero visible effort reads as more impressive than any reaction at all. Anime just gave the internet a huge, pre-existing library of clips that already fit that description.
faq: Why is Piccolo associated with aura farming?

Because his character is defined by staying calm and saying little even in extreme situations, which matches the aura farming template of doing something impressive without any visible effort or reaction.
What other characters show up in aura farming edits?
Gojo Satoru from Jujutsu Kaisen, Sung Jin Woo from Solo Leveling, and Agamemnon are the most common besides Piccolo, all for the same reason: calm confidence in the face of overwhelming power.
Is aura farming only an anime thing?
No, it started with a real video, not an anime clip. Anime characters became a popular subject for the edits afterward because they fit the format so well.

articles.title: How to Aura Farm: A Practical Guide | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: How to aura farm in real life: the step-by-step, the most common mistakes that cost you aura, and how to practice without overthinking it.
articles.answer: Aura farming in practice comes down to timing and silence: react calmly, don't explain what you did, and never look for a reaction from anyone. Break any of those three rules and you lose the aura instantly, no matter how impressive the original action was.
sections: The step-by-step
There's no real technique here — it's a habit you build. These are the four steps that show up in basically every clip:

ul: Let the moment happen. You can't plan aura farming in advance — the whole point is that the reaction looks natural.
React a beat late. An instant reaction reads as anxious. A short pause before you respond reads as control.
Don't look around afterward. The urge to check if anyone noticed is what kills the aura fastest. Keep moving like nothing happened.
Don't talk about it. If someone asks, say as little as possible. Explaining your own move is the quickest way to zero it out.

sections: Mistakes that cost you aura

ul: Sending a follow-up message explaining the first one.
Asking “did you see that?” after doing something cool.
Laughing at your own joke before you finish telling it.
Celebrating out loud over something small.
Asking someone to delete a photo of you — that guarantees more people see it.

faq: Can you actually practice aura farming on purpose?
Only up to a point — the core rule is that announcing you're aura farming cancels it out. The most you can practice is the habit of not explaining yourself and not checking for a reaction.
What's the single biggest mistake beginners make?
Celebrating. The most natural reaction after doing something well is to smile or comment on it — and that's exactly what zeroes out the aura in this meme.

articles.title: Aura Battles: What They Are, Where They Happen, How to Win | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: What an aura battle (or aura farming competition) actually is, where they've happened in real life, the unwritten rules, and how to actually win one.
articles.answer: An aura battle (also called an aura farming competition) is an informal face-off where two or more people take turns posing, making an entrance, or pulling off a move with total seriousness, and whoever's watching decides on the spot who has more aura. It started as something filmed for TikTok and ended up spilling into real life — actual aura battles have already happened in shopping malls, plazas, and schoolyards in multiple countries.
sections: What an aura battle actually is

It's the group, in-person version of the meme: instead of one person calmly reacting to an everyday situation, two or more people take turns doing poses, entrances, or choreographed moves, almost always with epic music playing. There's no real scoring or judge — whoever's watching decides on the spot, out loud, who walked away with more aura.

There's no organization behind it. The format started in schools and spread to the street as a game, then went viral on TikTok in 2025: someone posts a flyer with a time and place, people show up, and the round happens right there.
Where aura battles actually happen

Real aura battles have already been covered by news outlets in several cities. In Valencia, Spain, a group of teens organized one in a shopping mall and ended up moving to a nearby park after security broke it up; similar gatherings were reported in A Coruña. In Mexico, early videos showed friends putting together spontaneous battles of their own.
The pattern repeats everywhere: someone posts a TikTok flyer with a location and time, word spreads, and the actual event ends up smaller — and more improvised — than the final video suggests.
The unwritten rules
Nobody wrote these down anywhere, but almost every aura battle ends up following the same ones:

ul: Whoever laughs first during their own entrance loses automatically.
Explaining the pose afterward — "no wait, I was doing this because..." — is also an instant loss.
Epic background music isn't required, but it helps a lot.
The crowd votes out loud, by acclaim. Whoever shouts loudest wins the tiebreak.
Going in without any seriousness (clowning around on purpose) disqualifies you — the joke only works if you commit to it.

sections: How to win an aura battle
Winning has less to do with how elaborate your pose is and more to do with how little you seem to care about the outcome. A few things that show up in the battles that go well:

ul: Go in with something simple and commit to it completely. A complex pose that falls apart loses to a simple one held with total confidence.
Don't look for the crowd's reaction while you're posing. Checking whether people are filming or laughing costs you points instantly.
Hold something back for last. If everyone's doing the same thing, whoever closes with a variation wins the tiebreak.
If it goes wrong, don't fix it on the spot. Playing off a mistake like it was intentional gives you more aura than not messing up at all.

sections: The underlying rule is the same one from the original meme: whoever explains themselves, loses.
The online version: aura duels

Getting people together in person isn't always possible — that's where the site's aura duels come in as the online version of the exact same idea: instead of a crowd gathered in a park, anyone can jump in and vote on who has more aura, with the ranking updating live as votes come in.

There are three versions: everyday archetypes (who has more aura, the person who's always late or the one who replies way too fast?), historical figures (Cleopatra vs. Einstein), and celebrities. In all three, the winner of each duel steals points from the loser, exactly like a real battle — except the scoreboard actually sticks around.

articles.title: Aura Farming Glossary: Every Term Explained | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: Aura farming, aura points, negative aura, aura championship, 6-7, rizz: the complete glossary of meme terms, explained one by one.
articles.answer: This aura farming glossary collects and explains every term from the meme: from "aura farming" and "aura points" to the site's own modes, the aura championship, and the concepts it gets mixed up with, like "6-7" or "rizz".
sections: Core terms

dl: Aura farming
Building up charisma on purpose through actions that look effortless. The central verb of the whole meme: reacting well without explaining yourself or seeking anyone's approval.
Aura points
A fictional, made-up unit for measuring an action. There's no official scale — the convention is round, exaggerated numbers, both for gains and losses.
Having aura
Reacting well to a tough situation without showing effort or asking for anyone's reaction. The meme's ideal state.
Losing aura
The opposite of having aura: over-explaining, reacting badly, or fishing for approval after something happens.
Negative aura
A running total below zero after an embarrassing moment. Used as a joke, never seriously.
Aura bankruptcy
Extreme negative aura, when someone chains several mistakes together in a short time.
Aura farming kid
The internet nickname for Rayyan Arkan Dikha, the Indonesian kid from the canoe whose 2025 video started the meme.
Aura edits
Short videos that pair an everyday moment or an anime scene with epic music, framing calm or power as maximum effortlessness.
Infinite aura
An exaggeration of the concept describing someone (real or fictional) who never loses composure, as in the joke that certain athletes have infinite aura.

sections: Modes and formats on this site

dl: Gamer Mode
One of the site's three aura calculator modes, covering matches, voice chat, and win streaks.
School Mode
The calculator's school-themed mode: exams, presentations, hallways.
Party & Crush Mode
The mode for nights out and texts with a crush: the blue double check, 2 am messages, dancing at a party.
Aura championship
An informal pose-and-entrance contest that started in schools and went viral on TikTok in 2025. Whoever's watching decides who has more aura, on the spot and out loud.
Aura duel / aura battle
A one-on-one vote between two options — everyday archetypes, historical figures, or celebrities — where the winner steals aura points from the loser. The ranking updates live with every vote.
Gamer aura / football aura / anime aura
Themed variants of the same concept applied to gaming, football, and anime, each with its own test on the site.

sections: Related terms (and what they aren't)

dl: 6-7 / six seven
A different meme that circulated around the same time as aura farming and showed up in the same videos. It comes from a song and has no fixed meaning — it has no real connection to aura farming.
Rizz
A related but distinct meme: short for "charisma," and specifically about the ability to attract or flirt. Aura farming is broader — it applies to any situation, not just romantic ones.
Esoteric aura / aura colors
A supposed energy field with colors and spiritual meanings. It has no connection to TikTok's aura, which is purely a metaphor for charisma.
Main character energy
A related English-language phrase: acting like you're the protagonist of your own life. It overlaps partly with "having aura," but it's more about a general attitude than one specific reaction.

faq: Is aura farming the same as having rizz?
Not exactly. Both measure a form of charisma, but rizz is specifically about attracting or flirting, while aura farming applies to any everyday situation, not just romantic ones.
Where do all these terms come from?
Most of them started on TikTok in 2025, from Rayyan Arkan Dikha's viral video, and kept getting added as the meme spread to gaming, football, anime, and school life.
Is there an official list of aura farming terms?
There's no official organization behind any of this. This page collects the meme's most-used terms and gets updated as new ones show up.

articles.title: How to Organize an Aura Battle in Your City: The Complete Guide | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: A practical guide to running your own aura battle: step-by-step setup, a permits-and-safety checklist, social post and sign-up templates, and what to do if your city says no.
articles.h1: How to Organize an Aura Battle in Your City
articles.answer: Running an aura battle doesn't take much more than open space, a speaker, and people willing to compete without physical contact. What's worth sorting out beforehand is permission for the space, who runs the circle and calls the rounds, and what to do if your city says no — something that's already happened to several real battles in 2026. This guide covers all four, in order: the step-by-step for event day, the pre-event checklist, how to promote it, and what to learn from the battles that got blocked.
sections: Step by step: running the battle on the day
You don't need an official format — most real battles are put together by a group of friends or a social account with just this:

ul: Set the circle. An open space where people can stand around the edge without crowding the center. Plazas, wide sidewalks, or a school courtyard work better than a narrow street.
Bring the music. A portable speaker is enough. Music sets the pace for each round and cues the next competitor's turn.
Pick a host or MC. Someone to introduce each competitor, keep the order moving, and call it once the crowd has clearly decided. No mic needed if the group is small.
Set up the round format. The simplest version: straight elimination, one-on-one, 15-30 seconds per turn, crowd decides who moves on by applause or noise.
Decide how voting works. Crowd noise (an "applause-o-meter") is the most common — whoever gets the loudest reaction wins. No judges or scorecards needed.
Announce it with lead time. Post the place and time a day or two ahead — check the checklist below before you announce anything publicly.

sections: Checklist before the day
Go through this before you lock in a date, not the same day:

ul: Permission for the space. If it's a plaza, park, or other public space, check whether your city requires authorization — see the permits section below.
Location. Flat ground, good lighting if it's at night, and somewhere that won't block traffic or people who didn't come for the event.
Sound. A charged speaker (or a charger on hand) and a playlist ready to go.
Safety. Someone in charge who isn't competing, a circle that stays clear, and a plan for if more people show up than expected.
Age of participants. If minors are competing, make sure they're with an adult and the time slot fits their age.
Backup plan for rain or a closed venue. A nearby alternate spot in case the main one isn't available on the day.

sections: How to pick a location and get permission

A plaza or park is public space: using it for an organized event — even an informal one — usually means notifying your city, not just showing up and setting up the circle. This varies by city, but the pattern that repeated across the battles that got blocked in 2026 was always the same: the event was announced on social media before permission was confirmed in writing.

ul: Look up your city's parks, events, or public-space department (usually on the official website, or reachable by phone).
Ask for permission a few days ahead, not the night before — some cities have processes that take more than 24 hours.
If you get a yes, keep the confirmation in writing (email, text, whatever works) before you post the announcement.
If your main spot doesn't have confirmed permission in time, have a backup location (a wide sidewalk, a private courtyard) ready — that way you're not stuck depending on a single answer.

sections: Safety, minors, and public space
The aura battle format already comes with a built-in safety rule: no physical contact. Still, a few things are worth managing:

ul: Keep the circle clear of cars, bikes, and scooters — pick a spot where that's easy to control.
If minors are competing, have them come with an adult and keep the time slot appropriate for their age.
Put one person (not competing) in charge of the event: they cut it off if it gets tense, call time if things need to wrap up early, and are the point of contact if any authority shows up.
Don't oversell the event's scale — a group of friends competing in a plaza reads very differently to a city than a "championship" with paid sign-ups and hundreds of expected attendees.

sections: How to promote your battle on TikTok and Instagram
Most real battles filled up through social media, not flyers on the street:

ul: Post a short video announcing the date, time, and place, using whatever sound or meme is trending.
Tag the location so it shows up on that app's map.
Add trend hashtags (#auraFarming, #aurabattle) plus one specific to your event, so you can track reposts afterward.
Ask everyone who's already confirmed to share the post to their story — that's what actually brings real people, more than any paid boost.

sections: Copy-paste templates
Social post caption (swap out the brackets):

ul: "Aura battle at [location], [city] 🔥 [day], [date] at [time]. No sign-up, no physical contact, whoever's got the most aura wins. Bring your best pose. #auraFarming #aurabattle"

sections: The minimum info for a flyer or pinned post (save this as a text checklist):

ul: Event name and exact date/time.
Location with a clear landmark ("in front of [known spot]", not just an address).
Format: straight elimination, how voting works, how long each turn is.
Minimum age, or a note that minors need to come with an adult.
One contact (a handle or number) for questions before the event.

sections: Fields for a simple sign-up sheet (if your battle uses one):

ul: Name and social handle.
Age (and an emergency adult contact if a minor).
Emergency contact.
A checkbox for "I agree to compete with no physical contact and under the event's rules."

sections: What to do if your city won't authorize your event
It's already happened more than once in 2026, in different countries, always for the same reason: the event was announced in a public space before permission was confirmed.

ul: In Veracruz, Mexico, a municipal park blocked an aura battle for lacking authorization. Organizers didn't cancel — they moved the event to the sidewalk right outside the park instead.

In Niterói, Brazil, the city government blocked a "farmar aura" championship at Caminho Niemeyer because organizers never requested permission from the city's Events Coordination office — the venue was also already booked for something else the next day. Organizers rescheduled.
In Cuiabá, Brazil, the mayor directly vetoed the city's first "farmar aura" championship for lacking a permit to use the park — even so, a group ended up competing right in front of city hall.

sections: The lesson that repeats across all three: ask for permission before you announce the event, not alongside it. If you still get turned down, have a backup location ready (a wide sidewalk, a private space) instead of canceling outright — that's what all three battles above did, and none of them fell through completely.
faq: Do I need permission to run an aura battle in a plaza

It depends on the city, but as a general rule, yes — using public space for an organized event, even an informal one, usually means notifying your city's parks or events department. Getting that confirmed in writing before you announce on social media avoids the problem the Veracruz, Niterói, and Cuiabá battles ran into in 2026.
How many people do I need to run a battle

A small group is enough: two people competing and everyone else forming the circle that decides. Plenty of battles that went viral started exactly that way, with no sign-up or formal organizing at all.
How do you decide who wins each round
The most common method is crowd noise: one person competes at a time, and whoever gets the loudest reaction from the circle wins. No judges or scorecards required.
Can minors compete

Yes, as long as they come with a responsible adult and the event's time slot fits their age. The battle format itself has no physical contact, which makes it safer than a lot of other street-competition formats.
What do I do if my city won't give me a permit

Have a backup location planned ahead of time — a wide sidewalk or a private space near the original spot. In Veracruz and Cuiabá, when permission didn't come through, organizers moved the event a few steps from the original location instead of canceling.
Do I need money or sponsors to organize one
No. Most real battles ran on zero budget: a speaker, open space, and social media promotion is enough. Cash prizes show up in some bigger editions, but they're not a requirement of the format.

articles.title: Is It Safe to Farm Aura? Safety, Legality, and Advice for Schools | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: What the law says about organizing an aura battle, what happened when it went wrong in Mar del Plata, how universities and schools are handling it, and advice for parents and teachers.
articles.h1: Is It Safe to Farm Aura?
articles.answer: The aura farming meme jumped from TikTok to the street, and with it came questions a video can't answer: is it legal to gather people in a plaza, what happens when something goes wrong, and how should a school or a workplace handle it. In August 2026 a battle in Mar del Plata, Argentina ended with rocks being thrown, and that case — plus what's happened at universities and some workplaces — helps make sense of the real risks behind the game.
sections: Is it legal to organize or attend an aura battle?

There's no specific regulation for this in any country — there's no "aura battle law" — but the same rules that apply to any other use of public space still apply here. Spontaneously gathering in a plaza doesn't need a permit; announcing an event with a date, a place, and social media promotion, expecting a big turnout, usually does.
It's already happened more than once in 2026 that a battle got blocked for not having that permit:

ul: In Veracruz, Mexico, a municipal park banned an aura battle for lacking authorization. Organizers moved the event to the sidewalk right outside the park.
In Niterói, Brazil, the city government blocked a "farmar aura" championship because organizers never requested permission from the Events Coordination office.
In Cuiabá, Brazil, the mayor directly vetoed the city's first "farmar aura" championship for lacking a permit to use the park.

sections: If you're thinking about organizing a battle yourself, there's a full guide with the step-by-step for permits and safety: how to organize an aura battle.
When it went wrong: the Mar del Plata incident

On August 17, 2026, hundreds of teens gathered at Plaza Mitre in Mar del Plata, Argentina, for what became the first large-scale edition of the phenomenon in the country. Toward the end of the gathering, a group of adults unrelated to the battle — some accompanied by teenagers — started throwing rocks and bottles at participants, some of them laughing while they did it.

According to coverage, at least one person was hit, but no serious injuries were reported, police didn't intervene, and there were no arrests: the crowd dispersed and the event ended earlier than planned. Days later, a second edition was called at the same plaza, this time with organizers explicitly asking that the incidents not repeat.
The case shows the real risk of this kind of gathering: there's no official organization, no hired security, and anyone can join the ring of spectators — for better or worse.
What universities and schools are saying

No Argentine university organized, banned, or issued an official stance on aura battles in 2026, but the topic did reach the media through outside experts. Psychologist Martín Wainstein, a professor of Social Psychology at the University of Buenos Aires (UBA), put it this way: "Aura farming is a new name for something fairly old, which I'd define as the social production of prestige" (Infobae, August 19, 2026).
In other countries, battles did happen on university campuses — always organized by the students themselves, never by the institution:

ul: At USFQ (Universidad San Francisco de Quito, Ecuador), the first battle happened on August 27, 2026, in a courtyard on the Cumbayá campus, coming together spontaneously through social media.
At ESPOL (Escuela Superior Politécnica del Litoral, Ecuador), the August 21, 2026 gathering was, according to local coverage, "called by the students themselves, not by the institution."
At BUAP (Benemérita Universidad Autónoma de Puebla, Mexico), informal battles happened on the Rectory plaza, organized through a student call-out.

sections: The one body that did take a public stance was Costa Rica's Ministry of Education: its head, Leonardo Sánchez Hernández, clarified that "it isn't appropriate to ban or punish a youth expression solely because of what it's called," though schools can step in if the activity disrupts classes, creates dangerous crowding, or turns into humiliation or bullying toward a student.
A guide for schools and universities that want to run a controlled version

If an institution wants to give the trend a safe outlet instead of banning it outright, what shows up again and again in the editions that went well — inside and outside Argentina — comes down to a few points:

ul: Make it voluntary, never mandatory. No student should feel pressured to participate or even to watch.
One identified adult in charge. Someone (not a student) responsible for cutting the activity off if it gets tense, the same as you'd do for any other school event.
A time slot that doesn't interrupt classes. A long break, a free period, or after school hours — not in the middle of a class.
A defined, controlled space. A courtyard or gym with restricted access avoids the Mar del Plata problem: outsiders joining in with no control.
Clear rules from the announcement. No physical contact, no humiliating anyone, and anyone can drop out at any point with no pressure to stay.

sections: Is it a problem to skip work or class for this?

On the work side, there's already a public case in Argentina: a young man skipped work to compete in an aura battle, came in second, and was told his pay would be docked for the day. His response, quoted in several outlets: "If they actually do that, I'm going to sue them big time."

A Colombian labor lawyer, asked about the same issue, was more categorical: participating in or organizing aura battles during work hours can be treated as a breach of contract obligations, with a real risk of disciplinary action — especially if it happens repeatedly — and recommended doing it during lunch or after clocking out instead.

For schools, the clearest stance is still Costa Rica's Ministry of Education: no one should be punished just for farming aura, but the institution can act if the activity disrupts classes or creates a risky situation.
For parents and teachers: how to read the trend

To someone who doesn't know the meme, watching a group of teenagers pose silently in front of a crowd that's yelling can look stranger than it is. The experts consulted by the media read it in the same direction: it isn't a game with real points or an official competition, it's a new form — with video-game aesthetics — of something teenagers have always done: chase social status in front of their group.

In Spain, sociologist Tatiana Íñiguez-Berrozpe, of the University of Zaragoza, publicly analyzed one of the gatherings in her city in those same terms — as one more "neo-tribe," comparable to other youth trends that also looked baffling to the adults of their own time.

The no-physical-contact rule of the format makes it, in terms of physical safety, closer to posing for a photo than to a risky dare. What is worth keeping an eye on — and what Mar del Plata confirmed — is the safety of the location itself: avoiding spaces with no clear way out, with car traffic nearby, or where there's no way to control who joins in to watch.
faq: Is it legal to organize an aura battle in a plaza

It depends on the city, but as a general rule, yes, as long as you give advance notice to the public-space or events department. Announcing something with a date and heavy promotion without that notice is what got several battles blocked in 2026, in countries like Mexico and Brazil.
What happened at the Mar del Plata battle

On August 17, 2026, a large gathering at Plaza Mitre ended when a group of adults unrelated to the event threw rocks and bottles at participants. No serious injuries or arrests were reported, but the incident went viral as the most-cited example of how an aura battle can go wrong without organization or control of the space.
Did any university ban aura battles

In Argentina, no university took an official stance. In other countries, universities like USFQ, ESPOL, and BUAP had informal battles organized by their own students, without the institution banning or officially sponsoring them.
Can I have my pay docked for skipping work to farm aura

Legally, yes, the same as with any other unexcused absence: there's already a public case in Argentina of an employee being told his pay would be docked for the day. A labor lawyer consulted on the topic recommended avoiding work hours entirely and doing this kind of activity during lunch or after clocking out.
Can a school ban students from farming aura

Costa Rica's Ministry of Education, the body that took the clearest public stance, said no student should be punished just for participating, but that the institution can step in if the activity disrupts classes, creates dangerous crowding, or turns into bullying toward a student.
Is it physically dangerous to take part in an aura battle

The format itself has no physical contact, so the direct risk is low. The real risk, as the Mar del Plata case showed, is in the surroundings: an uncontrolled space that anyone can join, including people with nothing to do with the activity.
